article.body:
Consider a chef who tastes a dish mid-recipe to decide whether to add more salt or start over entirely. As an analogy, computer workers examine how artificial systems monitor their own choices during complex tasks. Our group is investigating how these systems allocate their mental effort between planning and execution. [1]

Team members 100, 101, 102, and 103 analyzed how reasoning models handle external oversight and multi-turn problems. Their recorded readings indicate that metareasoning governs how resources are split between planning and action. Paper-supported notes suggest that multi-turn models show distinct behavioral shifts under external supervision, while autonomous frameworks require self-generated goals to acquire flexible skills. [1, 2, 3, 4]

Meanwhile, teams 200, 201, 202, and 203 looked into epistemic self-correction and preference formation. Their findings highlight that inferential errors during preference updates are often path-dependent under misspecified models. Furthermore, recorded reviews emphasize that intrinsic self-correction remains fundamentally limited without external validation signals. [5, 6, 7, 8]

Rounding out the group, teams 300, 301, 302, and 303 explored curiosity-driven learning and multi-agent coordination. Their notebook records note that curiosity-driven strategies help agents explore complex problems with rare rewards, while structured communication dimensions improve joint performance across multiple units. [9, 10, 11, 12]

How can explicit falsification mechanisms be generalized across more diverse, unconstrained scientific domains when intrinsic correction falls short? [5]

Summary

We study how computer systems examine their reasoning using published papers. We look at resource management, preferences, and self-correction limits. We still do not know if systems can truly question their starting rules. We follow the Console as new readings arrive.
article.lede: We continue exploring how computer systems examine their own reasoning, tracking the shift from rigid calculations to flexible self-evaluation.
article.lens: Investigating the boundaries of automated reflection through shared source readings and safety frameworks.
article.title: Mapping the Machinery of Machine Reflection

Abstract
Hypotheses are central to information acquisi-
tion, decision-making, and discovery. However,
many real-world hypotheses are abstract, high-
level statements that are difficult to validate di-
rectly. This challenge is further intensified by
the rise of hypothesis generation from Large Lan-
guage Models (LLMs), which are prone to hallu-
cination and produce hypotheses in volumes that
make manual validation impractical. Here we
propose POPPER , an agentic framework for rigor-
ous automated validation of free-form hypotheses.
Guided by Karl Popper’s principle of falsifica-
tion, POPPER validates a hypothesis using LLM
agents that design and execute falsification exper-
iments targeting its measurable implications. A
novel sequential testing framework ensures strict
Type-I error control while actively gathering evi-
dence from diverse observations, whether drawn
from existing data or newly conducted procedures.
We demonstrate POPPER on six domains includ-
ing biology, economics, and sociology. POPPER
delivers robust error control, high power, and scal-
ability. Furthermore, compared to human scien-
tists, POPPER achieved comparable performance
in validating complex biological hypotheses while
reducing time by 10 folds, providing a scalable,
rigorous solution for hypothesis validation. POP-
PER is freely available at https://github.
com/snap-stanford/POPPER.

4.1. Results
POPPER achieves Type-I error control. Table 3 reports
the Type-I error rates and several key observations are in
order. First, most baselines fail to consistently control the
Type-I error, while POPPER remains below the nominal
level across all datasets. This underscores the necessity
of principled statistical design in LLM-driven hypothesis
validation; without such rigor, the flexibility of LLM agents
can inflate Type-I errors. Second, the comparison against
Fisher’s combined test highlights the benefits of e-values
in aggregating evidence. Third, the LLM-Likelihood Ratio
method lacks calibration, overly conservative for TargetVal-

6. Conclusion
We proposed POPPER , an LLM-based framework for val-
idating free-form hypotheses. By integrating a sequential
testing paradigm with automated experiment design and
execution, POPPER delivers scalable, statistically rigorous
hypothesis validation. This work represents an early explo-
ration, and several aspects can be further improved. Refining
test relevance and ensuring robust LLM implementations
remain challenges. Future work can also extend POPPER to
control other error metrics (e.g., false discovery rate), further
broadening its utility in scientific discovery and beyond.
Impact Statement
This work introduces POPPER , a statistically rigorous agen-
tic framework for hypothesis validation using Large Lan-
guage Model (LLM) agents. By combining advanced natu-
ral language processing capabilities with robust statistical
methodologies, POPPER addresses the critical challenge of
evaluating and validating hypotheses generated by LLMs,
ensuring that only evidence-backed hypotheses guide fu-
ture research. The broader implications of this work span
multiple domains, including biology, economics, and social
sciences, where hypothesis generation and validation play a
pivotal role in advancing knowledge.

Title:

Abstract:
Hypotheses are central to information acquisition, decision-making, and discovery. However, many real-world hypotheses are abstract, high-level statements that are difficult to validate directly. This challenge is further intensified by the rise of hypothesis generation from Large Language Models (LLMs), which are prone to hallucination and produce hypotheses in volumes that make manual validation impractical. Here we propose Popper, an agentic framework for rigorous automated validation of free-form hypotheses. Guided by Karl Popper's principle of falsification, Popper validates a hypothesis using LLM agents that design and execute falsification experiments targeting its measurable implications. A novel sequential testing framework ensures strict Type-I error control while actively gathering evidence from diverse observations, whether drawn from existing data or newly conducted procedures. We demonstrate Popper on six domains including biology, economics, and sociology. Popper delivers robust error control, high power, and scalability. Furthermore, compared to human scientists, Popper achieved comparable performance in validating complex biological hypotheses while reducing time by 10 folds, providing a scalable, rigorous solution for hypothesis validation.
